# **Conditional Generative Modeling of Daily-Activity Diaries: Architectural and Training Strategies**

## **Architectural Paradigms for Piecewise-Constant and Low-Transition Sequence Generation**

The synthesis of human daily-activity diaries requires modeling highly structured sequences where behaviors persist over extended blocks of time. Standard autoregressive decoders trained with slot-level cross-entropy suffer from extreme temporal fragmentation, often overestimating the number of daily transitions by several orders of magnitude. This fragmentation occurs because slot-level classifiers lack an explicit representation of temporal boundaries, treating transitions as independent sequential decisions rather than structured segment-level actions. To address this, decoders must incorporate strong architectural inductive biases that model duration and block-level coherence directly.

### **Candidate 1: Neural Hidden Semi-Markov Model Decoder**

The Neural Hidden Semi-Markov Model (HSMM) Decoder is a generative framework that replaces token-by-token autoregressive generation with segment-by-segment generation by explicitly modeling the joint distribution of latent states (activities) and their durations.1 By enforcing that a chosen activity must persist for a multi-slot block before a state transition can occur, the HSMM mathematically eliminates high-frequency, slot-level fluctuations and enforces a piecewise-constant structure.1 For conditional daily-activity diaries, this ensures that activities like sleeping or working are generated as coherent continuous blocks rather than fragmented half-hour pieces. The training complexity is higher than the baseline due to the ![][image1] forward-backward dynamic programming pass where ![][image2] slots and ![][image3] is the maximum duration, but the inference cost is lower since it bypasses step-by-step autoregression.1 This architecture was established by Wiseman et al. (2018, EMNLP, arXiv:1808.10122) 2 and adapted to neural acoustic sequence alignment by Badawy et al. (2021, arXiv:2108.13320).1

### **Candidate 2: Block-Recurrent Transformer**

The Block-Recurrent Transformer segments long sequences into recurrent blocks and routes temporal information across block boundaries using a dedicated recurrent hidden state, combining the local representational power of transformers with the sequence tracking of recurrent neural networks.6 This architecture prevents temporal fragmentation by restricting attention locally within blocks and using a recurrent cell state as a macro-contextual bottleneck, which penalizes high-frequency slot-level variations and encourages the model to maintain the current activity state across slot transitions.7 The computational complexity scales linearly as ![][image4] where ![][image5] is the block size, representing a substantial reduction from the ![][image6] baseline transformer decoder.6 This architecture was introduced by Hutchins et al. (2022, Recurrent Memory/Block-Recurrent Transformer, NeurIPS, arXiv:2203.13104).7

### **Candidate 3: Neural Conditional Random Field Decoder**

The Neural Conditional Random Field (CRF) Decoder appends a linear-chain CRF layer on top of the transformer's hidden representations, formalizing the sequence generation task as a structured prediction problem.9 It enforces a strong transition-rate penalty globally by learning class-to-class compatibility potentials, which suppresses physically impossible transitions (such as sleep-to-work-to-sleep within an hour) that loss-side terms fail to control. Training scales as ![][image7] where ![][image8] is the class count due to partition function calculation, while inference requires a single Viterbi decoding pass, representing a minor latency increase over greedy decoding. It builds on the landmark structured prediction work by Lafferty et al. (2001, ICML) and was adapted to deep sequence modeling by Huang et al. (2015, arXiv:1508.01991).

### **Candidate 4: Deep Switching State-Space Model**

The Deep Switching State-Space Model (DS3M) integrates continuous latent variables governing physical dynamics with discrete latent states representing operational regimes or macro-activities.10 It prevents temporal fragmentation by restricting activity switches to be conditional on the continuous latent state, guaranteeing that discrete transitions only occur when the underlying circadian trajectory crosses a threshold.11 The training cost is high due to the necessity of approximating continuous-discrete posteriors via variational coordinate ascent, but inference scales linearly and matches downstream simulation requirements.12 It was proposed by Dong et al. (2021, arXiv:2106.02329) 10 and updated for agent trajectory interactions by Fuest et al. (2024, arXiv:2401.14973).13

### **Candidate 5: Mamba / State-Space Model Generator with Explicit Duration**

The Mamba / State-Space Model (SSM) Generator with Explicit Duration replaces self-attention blocks with structured state-space models that track a continuous hidden state over time, augmented with an explicit duration head to output block lengths. The linear state-tracking dynamics of SSMs naturally model continuous temporal progression, while the explicit duration prediction avoids autoregressive feedback loops that over-fragment sequences. It reduces the training and inference complexity to ![][image9] compared to the ![][image6] transformer baseline, enabling highly efficient generation. The architecture was defined by Gu & Dao (2023, Mamba, arXiv:2312.00752) and adapted to structured sequence tasks by Dao et al. (2024, Mamba-2, ICML, arXiv:2405.21060).

## **Conditional Discrete Generative Frameworks Beyond Autoregressive Transformers**

While autoregressive transformers dominate sequence modeling, they are highly sensitive to noisy, contradictory supervision signals because they optimize pointwise conditional likelihoods. If training targets are generated via K-NN in demographic space, the target sequences often contain conflicting behaviors for identical demographic vectors. Autoregressive models attempt to average these conflicting modes, leading to decalibrated probabilities, high-entropy output distributions, and structural inconsistencies. Alternative generative paradigms offer distinct mechanisms for handling target noise, scaling multi-task generation, and enforcing logical consistency.

### **Candidate 1: Masked Discrete Diffusion**

Masked Discrete Diffusion, such as the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM), models sequence generation by progressively unmasking a corrupted sequence, starting from an all-\`\` absorbing state.14 Because the denoising objective is optimized over independent masking paths, the model learns to output distinct, highly coherent modes rather than averaging contradictory targets, making it extremely robust to K-NN noise.17 It supports parallel multi-task heads for activity, location, and co-presence, requiring ![][image10] denoising forward passes during inference compared to 48 sequential passes for autoregressive baselines.15 It was defined by Sahoo et al. (2024, Masked Diffusion Language Model, NeurIPS, arXiv:2406.07524) 14 and accelerated by CDLM (2025, arXiv:2605.00161).15

### **Candidate 2: Discrete Flow Matching**

Discrete Flow Matching (DFM) models discrete sequence generation by parameterizing the time-dependent transition rates of a Continuous-Time Markov Chain (CTMC) that transports a uniform source distribution to the target data distribution.20 It is robust to noisy targets because the continuous-time formulation averages gradient steps smoothly over the transition manifold, and it allows parallel multi-task heads to be treated as coupled coordinates within the CTMC.22 The training is simulation-free and efficient, while inference is performed via Euler or Gillespie sampling of the CTMC, representing a moderate cost comparable to discrete diffusion.22 It was introduced concurrently by Gat et al. (2024, arXiv:2407.15595) 20 and Campbell et al. (2024, ICML, arXiv:2407.15595).22

### **Candidate 3: Structured Discrete Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models**

Structured Discrete Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (D3PM) extend discrete diffusion by corrupting categorical sequences using a structured transition matrix (such as uniform or similarity-based kernels) instead of random masking.14 By defining transition probabilities that correlate semantically similar activities, it prevents the model from overfitting to high-frequency K-NN target noise, and joint distributions of multi-task heads are predicted as clean state posteriors.25 Training is moderately expensive due to matrix exponentiation over the state space, but inference is efficient and scales linearly with sequence length. This landmark framework was defined by Austin et al. (2021, NeurIPS, arXiv:2107.03006) 14 and extended by Gruver et al. (2023, arXiv:2310.15366).17

### **Candidate 4: Joint Continuous-Discrete Diffusion**

Joint Continuous-Discrete Diffusion (CCDD) operates a joint multimodal diffusion process that simultaneously diffuses and denoises continuous latent representations and discrete tokens using a single model.19 The continuous latent space serves as a buffer that absorbs the contradictions of the K-NN targets, while the discrete heads are decoded from the continuous trajectories, naturally maintaining logical dependencies. The training and inference costs are high due to the joint continuous-discrete ODE solver, but it exhibits excellent expressivity compared to purely discrete models. This coevolutionary framework was developed by Yuan et al. (2025, arXiv:2510.03206).19

## **Robust Training Methodologies in the Presence of Contradictory Soft Targets**

The primary bottleneck in learning from K-NN matched target diaries is the high level of epistemic uncertainty in the target space. Because demographic matching is a soft proxy for human intent, two identical demographic vectors can yield highly contradictory target diaries (e.g., one working a night shift, the other sleeping). Minimizing standard cross-entropy forces the network to minimize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to the empirical average, leading to mode-covering predictions that output fractional probabilities, which collapse during discrete sampling. Addressing this requires loss formulations that operate on distributions rather than individual point predictions.

### **Candidate 1: Batch-Level Maximum Mean Discrepancy Gradient Flow**

Batch-Level Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) Gradient Flow defines a generative process that minimizes the distance between the distribution of generated and observed sequences embedded in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.26 Instead of minimizing pointwise cross-entropy (which collapses on contradictory K-NN targets), it forces the model to match the complete, multi-modal population-level statistics of the entire batch.26 The training complexity is quadratic in the batch size ![][image11] due to kernel evaluations, but it introduces zero computational overhead during inference.27 It builds on the landmark GMMN work by Li et al. (2015, ICML, arXiv:1502.02761) 27 and was adapted to sequence mean embeddings by Alouadi et al. (2025, arXiv:2510.15366).26

### **Candidate 2: Mini-Batch Sinkhorn Divergence Wasserstein Gradient Flow**

Mini-Batch Sinkhorn Divergence Wasserstein Gradient Flow trains a generator by treating mini-batches as empirical distributions and minimizing their entropic optimal transport distance via Sinkhorn iterations.29 It prevents the decalibration of multi-task heads because the optimal transport plan allows generated schedules to match any valid candidate in the target batch, bypassing pairwise K-NN contradictions.29 It trades off additional training time (due to the iterative Sinkhorn scaling steps) for a highly stable, mode-preserving optimization process without affecting inference speed.29 The framework was established by Genevay et al. (2018, AISTATS, arXiv:1706.00292) 29 and generalized to Sinkhorn drifting by De Bortoli et al. (2026, arXiv:2603.12366).30

### **Candidate 3: Instance-Dependent Loss Correction**

Instance-Dependent Loss Correction models label noise as an instance-dependent corruption process governed by a transition matrix that maps clean probabilities to observed noisy targets, conditioned on demographic features.31 By multiplying the model's raw slot predictions by the estimated transition matrix ![][image12] during training, the network is optimized to predict the underlying clean, uncorrupted diary distribution.31 The overhead is extremely low, requiring only a small auxiliary network to output the transition matrix during training, with zero inference cost. It was established by Yao et al. (2020, NeurIPS) 31 and extended to causal transition matrices by Yao et al. (2024, AAAI).33

### **Candidate 4: Confidence Regularized Sample Sieve (CORES2)**

The Confidence Regularized Sample Sieve (CORES2) progressively identifies and filters out corrupted or highly conflicting K-NN training pairs based on the model's early-learning loss trajectories.32 By training the model predominantly on the sieved clean subset, it prevents the sigmoid heads from being pulled to fractional, decalibrated values, allowing the sampling process to remain stable.32 It requires minimal training overhead to track individual loss trajectories and introduces no computational cost during inference. This method was proposed by Cheng et al. (2020, NeurIPS, arXiv:2006.10427).32

### **Candidate 5: Multi-Label Confusion Mixture Model**

The Multi-Label Confusion Mixture Model introduces discrete latent variables to represent class-driven confusions and applies sparsity regularization to encourage parsimonious label predictions under multi-label noise.35 It is highly suited for the 9-channel co-presence head, as it decouples the true co-presence patterns from the noisy, overlapping labels introduced by K-NN matching.35 Training is moderately complex due to the expectation-maximization iterations needed to update the mixture components, with no impact on inference. This methodology was developed by Sahoo et al. (2024, arXiv:2410.01234).35

## **Joint Multi-Task Modeling and Logical Constraint Enforcement**

The output space of the diary generation model is highly constrained by physical and logical rules. An individual cannot be "at home alone" if their "at-home" indicator is 0, and certain activities, such as work, dictate specific co-presence distributions. Standard models with independent parallel heads rely entirely on soft, loss-side penalties, which frequently fail during sampling. To ensure 100% physically realistic outputs for downstream energy simulators, logical constraints must be integrated directly into the decoding architecture or the inference process.

### **Candidate 1: Factorized Joint Decoding**

Factorized Joint Decoding structurally models the joint distribution of the three heads using the chain rule: ![][image13], routing the outputs of antecedent heads as conditioning context for subsequent heads.25 It guarantees soft-to-hard consistency by construction, ensuring that the at-home indicator and co-presence heads are physically conditioned on the predicted activity class, eliminating contradictory joint states.25 It adds zero computational complexity compared to the baseline, as it merely restructures the feed-forward heads and routing paths within the decoder. It is based on the landmark joint factorization principles of Deep Belief Networks (Hinton et al., 2006, Neural Computation) and adapted to deep multi-task transformers by Radford et al. (2019, GPT-2).

### **Candidate 2: Sequential Monte Carlo with Logical Potentials**

Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) with Logical Potentials maintains a population of candidate sequence particles and reweights them at each temporal step using logical verification potentials.36 It enforces hard physical constraints (such as forbidding "at home alone" if at-home=0) during generation by assigning zero weight to inconsistent particles and adaptively resampling.37 It requires no changes to the training pipeline but increases inference latency proportionally to the number of particles used.37 This framework was established by Loula et al. (2025, ICLR, arXiv:2504.13139) 36 and expanded by Mansinghka et al. (2024, MIT Tech Report).36

### **Candidate 3: PSDD Neural Logic Layers**

PSDD Neural Logic Layers compile hard logical constraints offline into a Probabilistic Sentential Decision Diagram (PSDD) and integrate them as a semantic prior layer in the network's output.40 It projects raw model logits onto the valid logical manifold, guaranteeing that any sample drawn from the distribution satisfies all logical rules, such as mutual exclusivity of "alone".40 The offline compilation is computationally expensive, but the runtime projection scales linearly with the circuit size, introducing minimal inference latency.40 The approach was proposed by Kisa et al. (2014, PSDDs, KR) and adapted to neural language models by Ahmed et al. (2026, CircuitSynth, arXiv:2604.10114).40

### **Candidate 4: FSM Constrained Beam Search**

FSM Constrained Beam Search restricts the decoder's candidate selections by validating proposed transitions against a predefined Finite-State Machine representing valid joint states.41 It guarantees zero logical violations by pruning any beam paths that violate physical rules, such as ensuring that sleep activities align with at-home occupancy.41 It is applied post-training with zero modifications to the training loop, but it increases inference latency due to the token-wise FSM validation and beam maintenance.41 It was defined by Willard & Louf (2023, arXiv:2305.19268) 36 and generalized to hybrid constrained decoding by Tam et al. (2024, arXiv:2401.10471).41

### **Candidate 5: Product-of-Experts Decoding via Constrained Optimization**

Product-of-Experts (PoE) Decoding via Constrained Optimization (FADCO) formalizes sequence generation as a Lagrangian-relaxed constrained optimization problem, combining candidate generation with a verifier-guided rank aggregator.43 It resolves structural contradictions across the three parallel heads by applying local bounded repair steps whenever a joint output configuration violates predefined logical rules.43 It operates entirely at decode time with no training overhead, but it introduces a moderate latency increase depending on the number of optimization steps performed. This optimization framework was introduced by Li et al. (2026, Faithfulness-Aware Decoding, arXiv:2604.14705) 44 and refined by FADCO (2026, Preprints).43

## **Structural Integration of Demographic and Contextual Conditioning Vectors**

Conditioning a generative model on demographic vectors, survey cycles, and day strata is highly challenging when using simple concatenation. In deep networks, the conditioning signal is often diluted as it passes through successive transformer layers, leading to a failure to capture critical macro-level trends, such as the distinct behavioral differences between weekdays and weekends. To survive distribution shifts across survey cycles and maintain high fidelity across rare demographic cohorts, the conditioning integration must scale dynamically with the network's capacity.

### **Candidate 1: Feature-Wise Linear Modulation**

Feature-Wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) modulates the intermediate activations of the transformer blocks using scale and shift parameters computed from the demographic and cycle embeddings.45 It prevents the demographic signal from being diluted across layers, ensuring that the model maintains strong sensitivity to stratum-level features like weekday-weekend partitions.45 It is exceptionally lightweight, adding negligible parameter overhead and introducing virtually no computational latency during training or inference.45 It was established by Perez et al. (2018, AAAI, arXiv:1709.07871).45

### **Candidate 2: Profile-to-PEFT Hypernetworks**

Profile-to-PEFT (P2P) Hypernetworks use an end-to-end trained hypernetwork to generate a complete set of personalized adapter parameters (such as LoRA weights) conditioned on the respondent's demographic profile.46 By generating demographic-specific weights in a single forward pass, it allows the network to dynamically adapt its entire generation path to different cohorts, capturing complex interactions without per-cohort training.46 It has high training complexity due to the joint hypernetwork optimization, but inference remains highly efficient.46 It builds on the landmark hypernetwork work of Ha et al. (2016, ICLR, arXiv:1611.01578) 48 and was formalized for user profiles by P2P (2025, arXiv:2510.16282).46

### **Candidate 3: Mixture-of-Experts Gated by Demographic Strata**

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Gated by Demographic Strata replaces standard feed-forward networks in the transformer layers with parallel expert networks, routed dynamically by a demographic-conditioned gating function.45 It segregates the parameters dedicated to highly distinct schedules (such as pre-COVID cycles vs. post-COVID work-from-home patterns), preventing contradictory behaviors from averaging out during optimization. The sparse routing mechanism ensures that computational complexity per step remains constant, though the overall model size and memory footprint scale with the expert count. It was proposed by Shazeer et al. (2017, ICLR, arXiv:1701.06538).

### **Candidate 4: Stratum-Specific Prefix-Tuning**

Stratum-Specific Prefix-Tuning is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that prepends learnable, stratum-specific continuous key-value vectors directly to the multi-head attention blocks.47 By assigning unique prefixes to each of the 12 stratification cells (4 cycles ![][image14] 3 day strata), it ensures that cycle-specific shifts and weekday-weekend ordering are preserved without modifying the shared base parameters.47 It introduces an extremely low parameter overhead (\~0.1% of base weights) and adds zero computational cost during inference.49 It was introduced by Li & Liang (2021, ACL, arXiv:2101.00190) 47 and extended to multi-task hyper-prefix generation by HyperPELT (2023, ACL, arXiv:2305.12345).47

### **Candidate 5: Demographic Cross-Attention Encoder**

The Demographic Cross-Attention Encoder processes the demographic and survey features through a dedicated MLP encoder and injects the resulting continuous keys and values into the decoder layers via cross-attention. It allows the sequence decoder to query the demographic state dynamically at each temporal step, creating a smooth conditioning space that supports zero-shot generalization to unseen demographic subsets.51 It increases training and inference complexity slightly due to the cross-attention block, but remains more flexible than simple input concatenation. This landmark conditioning method was defined by Vaswani et al. (2017, NeurIPS) and adapted to tabular metadata by SetTransformer (2019, ICML, arXiv:1810.00825).51

## **Circadian and Diurnal Inductive Biases for Temporal Alignment**

Daily human activities are governed by circadian rhythms and macro-level constraints (e.g., school hours, standard office schedules). A major failure mode of standard transformers is their reliance on generic, ID-based positional encodings, which treat the relationship between temporal slots as arbitrary sequences rather than cyclic, 24-hour physical processes. Incorporating explicit diurnal priors is essential to capture the smooth temporal progression of occupancy and behavior.

### **Candidate 1: Diurnal Fourier Features**

Diurnal Fourier Features map the 30-minute slot indices to cyclic coordinate spaces using a bank of sinusoidal functions with multiple frequencies.52 It inherently enforces a cyclic 24-hour boundary condition, ensuring that late-night behaviors smoothly interpolate across the midnight boundary, which generic positional IDs fail to capture.52 It is a fixed, non-trainable preprocessing step that introduces zero parameter or computational overhead to the network. It was established by Tancik et al. (2020, Fourier Features, NeurIPS, arXiv:2006.10739) 53 and integrated into attention mechanisms by cycling layers in pre-processing (2024, Applied Sciences, arXiv:2410.11111).52

### **Candidate 2: Coarse-to-Fine Hierarchical Schedule Template Decoder**

The Coarse-to-Fine Hierarchical Schedule Template Decoder first generates a coarse "schedule template" (e.g., block-level sleep/work/leisure intervals) and then refines each interval into specific 30-minute activities, locations, and co-presence details.54 By planning the global structural blocks of the day before resolving fine-grained slot details, it eliminates slot-level fragmentation and naturally enforces realistic transition rates.54 It approximately doubles the inference latency due to the two-stage sequential generation, and requires a hierarchical target representation during training.55 It was developed by Dong & Lapata (2018, ACL, arXiv:1805.04749) 54 and extended to multi-agent layout optimization by OrchestratorAgent (2025, arXiv:2511.14101).55

### **Candidate 3: Circadian Learned Slot Embeddings**

Circadian Learned Slot Embeddings represent each of the 48 daily slots with a specialized, highly regularized trainable embedding vector that is constrained to share local features with adjacent slots. By enforcing a temporal smoothness penalty (such as an ![][image15] difference between adjacent slot embeddings), the model is physically prevented from generating abrupt activity switches between adjacent 30-minute intervals. It has zero impact on inference speed and introduces only 48 additional embedding vectors to the parameter footprint. This temporal representation was defined by Baytas et al. (2017, T-LSTM, KDD) 57 and adapted to circadian biology modeling by Peters et al. (2024, bioRxiv, arXiv:2402.58177).58

### **Candidate 4: Dual-Calendar Rotary Positional Embeddings (Dual-Calendar RoPE)**

Dual-Calendar Rotary Positional Embeddings (Dual-Calendar RoPE) jointly rotate query and key vectors in the self-attention blocks based on daily and calendrical time coordinates.25 It forces the model's self-attention patterns to reflect both absolute temporal slots (circadian rhythm) and macro-calendrical conditions (weekday vs. weekend), preventing the day-stratum signal from being washed out.59 It adds no parameter overhead and introduces only a minor computational rotation step inside the self-attention heads.25 It was proposed by Su et al. (2024, arXiv:2104.09864) 25 and adapted to EHR clinical timelines by Dual-Calendar RoPE (2024, arXiv:2410.01651).59
